title: Early Layer Safety vs. Late Layer Safety: Which Layers' Representations Actually Determine Refusal

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: identifying the causally necessary vs merely correlated layers for safety behavior makes evaluations more reliable and interventions more precise, directly improving the efficiency of alignment work.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Training linear probes at every layer and performing residual stream patching layer-by-layer are well-documented intermediate TransformerLens operations. Systematic but guided CS students can manage this.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: train probes at every layer, patch each layer with a 'will not refuse' forward pass, identify minimal causally necessary layer set. Clear experimental protocol with measurable outcomes.

novelty.reasoning: 'Safety Layers in Aligned Large Language Models: The Key to LLM Security' (ICLR 2025) identifies safety layers as a small set of contiguous layers in the middle (14-25% of network depth), distinct from answer prediction layers. 'The Geometry of Refusal: Concept Cones and Representational Independence' (2025) reveals multiple independent refusal directions and concept cones rather than a single direction. 'LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately' (2025) shows harmfulness is encoded at earlier positions and refusal at later positions. 'Understanding and Mitigating Over-refusal via Safety Representation' (2025) shows over-refusal stems from shortcut keyword detection in lower layers. The core question of which layers are causally necessary for refusal is substantially answered.
